Elegy

EL-uh-jee · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Elegy is a poem of serious reflection, typically a lament for the dead.

The poet wrote an elegy for her grandfather, weaving together memories of his garden with reflections on mortality.

Worked Example

For his final project, the student composed an elegy honoring the town's oldest oak tree, cut down after a storm, reflecting on everything it had witnessed over two hundred years.

An elegy is a written poem of thoughtful mourning -- it doesn't have to be about a person; it can mourn a place, an era, or even a tree.

How Elegy Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

ode

ode: a poem, often reflective, addressed to a particular subject

requiem

requiem: a piece of music or verse composed to honor the dead

Antonyms

toast

toast: a short speech in celebration of someone or something

jubilee

jubilee: a celebration of an anniversary, marked by great joy

How Strong Is It? — reflection → elegy → mourning

reflection vs. elegy

reflection vs. elegy: A quiet reflection is any thoughtful pause, not necessarily written down or about death.

mourning vs. elegy

mourning vs. elegy: Deep mourning goes beyond writing a reflective poem -- it's the full, immediate grief itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — elegos

root — elegos: a mournful poem or song of lament (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Elegy comes directly from Greek elegos, a mournful poem or song of lament -- the ancient Greek word for exactly this kind of reflective mourning poem.

Use the root in a new word: elegiac

Use the root in a new word: elegiac: Critics described the film's slow, reflective final scene as elegiac, mourning a way of life that no longer exists.

Word Building

Word Choice

An elegy is written reflection, often about death or loss -- similar to this unit's own word dirge, which is a mournful piece specifically meant to be sung or performed, while an elegy is typically read as a poem.
